stem:
Spot the Voice Shift

Which of the following sentences is written in passive voice?

options.label: A
options.text: Churchill rallied the nation with his speeches.

options.label: B
options.text: The nation was rallied by Churchill's speeches.

options.label: C
options.text: Churchill's speeches rallied an entire nation.

options.label: D
options.text: "We shall fight on the beaches," Churchill declared.

explanation: "The nation was rallied" places the receiver of the action (the nation) in the subject position. The other three options all use active constructions where the doer leads the sentence.

stem:
Name That Sentence Type

"It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness." (Charles Dickens, *A Tale of Two Cities*)

What sentence type is this?
explanation: Dickens chains together multiple independent clauses joined by commas. Each clause could stand alone as its own sentence, making this a compound structure (and a famously long one).

stem:
Punctuation Personality

A writer consistently uses short, punchy sentences. Periods everywhere. Rarely a comma in sight. What does this punctuation pattern signal?

options.label: D
options.text: A writer who hasn't learned comma rules yet

explanation: Frequent periods create a staccato rhythm that reads as decisive and direct. This is a deliberate stylistic choice, not a grammar gap. Hemingway built an entire career on it.

stem:
The Power of Repetition

"I have a dream that one day this nation will rise up... I have a dream that one day on the red hills of Georgia... I have a dream that my four little children..." (Martin Luther King Jr.)

What rhetorical device is King using here?
explanation: Anaphora is the repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of successive clauses. King repeats "I have a dream" to build emotional momentum, making each new vision land harder than the last.

stem:
The Mirror Flip

"Ask not what your country can do for you; ask what you can do for your country." (John F. Kennedy)

This famous line is an example of:
explanation: Antimetabole repeats words in reverse order to create a contrasting meaning. Kennedy flips "country/you" into "you/country," turning a passive expectation into an active call to duty.

stem:
The Rule of Three

"Government of the people, by the people, for the people." (Abraham Lincoln, Gettysburg Address)

This structure is called:
explanation: A tricolon is a series of three parallel elements. Lincoln's three prepositional phrases build on each other and create a rhythm that feels complete. Two would feel unfinished. Four would feel like a list.

stem:
Seeing Is Believing

"All the world's a stage, and all the men and women merely players." (William Shakespeare, *As You Like It*)

What device is Shakespeare using?
explanation: Shakespeare doesn't say the world is *like* a stage (that would be a simile). He says it *is* a stage, making a direct equivalence. That direct claim is what makes a metaphor hit harder than a comparison.

stem:
The Elegant Reversal

"Let us never negotiate out of fear, but let us never fear to negotiate." (John F. Kennedy)

This is another example of which device?
explanation: Chiasmus reverses the grammatical structure of a parallel phrase. "Negotiate/fear" flips into "fear/negotiate," creating a balanced, memorable contrast. It is closely related to antimetabole but focuses on structure rather than exact word repetition.

stem:
Match the Register

You are writing a product announcement for a Fortune 500 company's investor relations page. Which opening line fits the context best?

options.label: A
options.text: "Hey everyone, we just dropped something huge."

options.label: B
options.text: "We are pleased to announce the launch of our next-generation platform."

options.label: C
options.text: "YOU WON'T BELIEVE WHAT WE JUST BUILT."

options.label: D
options.text: "So yeah, we made a thing. It's pretty cool."

explanation: Investor relations requires a formal register that signals professionalism and credibility. Options A and D are too casual, and C reads like clickbait. The formal tone in B matches what that audience expects.

stem:
Reading the Room

A nonprofit sends a fundraising email that opens: "Per our analysis of quarterly giving trends, we are requesting a contribution to sustain operational capacity."

What is wrong with this tone?

options.label: C
options.text: It sounds like a corporate memo, not a human asking for help

options.label: D
options.text: Nothing. This is exactly how fundraising should sound.

explanation: Fundraising works through emotional connection and personal storytelling. This opening reads like an internal budget report. The language creates distance when the goal is to bring the reader closer.

stem:
Tone Detective

Read these two sentences and identify the tonal shift:

Version A: "We're rethinking how teams collaborate."
Version B: "The way teams collaborate is broken."

What is the primary difference in tone?

options.label: A
options.text: Version A is optimistic and forward-looking; Version B is confrontational and urgent

options.label: B
options.text: Version A is formal; Version B is casual

options.label: C
options.text: They say the same thing in the same tone

options.label: D
options.text: Version A is passive; Version B is active

explanation: Both sentences address the same topic, but Version A frames it as opportunity while Version B frames it as a problem. That framing choice changes the emotional response completely, even though the underlying message is similar.

stem:
The Opening Move

"It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife." (Jane Austen, *Pride and Prejudice*)

What makes this opening line effective as a voice signature?

options.label: B
options.text: It uses irony to immediately establish the author's sharp, satirical perspective

options.label: C
options.text: It asks the reader a direct question

options.label: D
options.text: It uses emotional language to create sympathy

explanation: Austen opens with a statement that sounds like universal truth but is actually dripping with irony. Nobody actually believes this is universally acknowledged. That gap between what is said and what is meant tells you everything about the voice you are about to spend 300 pages with.

stem:
Story Structure as Identity

A brand always opens its case studies with a specific client's name, a concrete problem, and the exact moment things changed. This pattern is an example of:

options.label: B
options.text: A signature narrative structure that builds trust through consistency

explanation: Repeating a narrative structure across content creates recognition. The audience learns what to expect, and that predictability becomes part of the brand's identity. Consistency in storytelling is a voice decision, not a limitation.

stem:
Pick the Winner

You are writing a landing page headline for busy startup founders. Which option will perform best?

options.label: A
options.text: "Our Comprehensive Suite of Integrated Solutions for Scaling Organizations"

options.label: C
options.text: "A Thoroughly Researched Approach to Organizational Growth Metrics"

options.label: D
options.text: "Welcome to our website! We do lots of things for lots of people."

explanation: Startup founders are time-starved and action-oriented. Short, punchy, benefit-driven language matches their mindset. The other options are either too vague, too corporate, or too generic to earn a second glance.

stem:
Context Is Everything

A law firm needs to send an email to a client whose case just had a major setback. Which draft strikes the right balance?

options.label: A
options.text: "Hey! So, bad news. We lost the motion. But don't worry, it'll be fine. LOL."

options.label: B
options.text: "After careful review of today's ruling, we want to walk you through what happened, what it means for your case, and the options ahead."

options.label: C
options.text: "Pursuant to the adjudicatory proceedings of the aforementioned date, the tribunal rendered a disposition adverse to the petitioner's motion."

explanation: A legal setback requires a tone that is honest, calm, and structured. Option A is wildly inappropriate. Option C buries the message in jargon. Option D is too blunt for a sensitive moment. Option B acknowledges the situation and immediately offers a path forward.
